newsitem.title: USA: Find out how your broker is paid, SEC chief warns.
newsitem.headline: Find out how your broker is paid, SEC chief warns.

text.p: To help avoid scams and losses, the nation's top securities regulator Monday urged investors to ask their brokers how they get paid for the investment products they pitch.

"Commissions reward a broker for the quantity of his transactions, not necessarily the quality," Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt said in prepared remarks to some 800 indviduals attending the agency's "town meeting" in Tulsa, Okla.
The speech is due to be delivered at 6 p.m. EDT (2200 GMT) Monday.
Levitt cautioned that some Wall Street compensation practices, including sales contests, may drive brokers to sell stocks that are in the interest of the broker rather than the investor.
These sales contests, Levitt said, often are sponsored by third parties who are anxious to move a product.

"Contests are not inherently bad, but they have the potential to focus the broker on something other than the needs of the human being in front of him," Levitt said in his remarks, which were made available to reporters.

Levitt, who for years now has been aggressively campaigning to educate investors, said his agency will fight to discourage sales contests and other programmes that reward brokers for high volume sales rather than good service.
Putting an end to the practice is going to be a high priority for the SEC over the next year, Levitt told Reuters in a recent interview.
"Some firms are doing better than others, but I think they have further to go," Levitt said, indicating he may seek more disclosure from firms about their broker compensation plans.
"The very practice of disclosure would discourage the practice," Levitt said of the sales contests and other ploys used to encourage big volume sales.
But investors too, must help put an end to these popular Wall Street customs, Levitt said.

"The SEC can and will demand that standards of practice in the industry be higher. But if firms hear that same demand also coming from you as investors, change will come sooner," Levitt told the investor group Monday.
